reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD
clinicalPearls: The hepatic porphyrias are inherited or acquired defects of haem biosynthesis in which pathway intermediates accumulate and cause acute neurovisceral attacks or cutaneous disease

Acute intermittent porphyria, the most common acute form, presents with severe unexplained abdominal pain, autonomic disturbance, hyponatraemia, and neuropsychiatric features, without skin involvement
Attacks are precipitated by many drugs, fasting or crash dieting, alcohol, infection, and hormonal fluctuations, so a careful trigger history is essential
During an acute attack the urine contains excess porphobilinogen and delta-aminolaevulinic acid and may darken on standing
Porphyria cutanea tarda, the most common porphyria overall, causes photosensitive skin fragility and blistering and is strongly linked with hepatitis C, alcohol, iron overload, and oestrogen use
The acute porphyrias carry an increased long-term risk of hepatocellular carcinoma, warranting surveillance in older patients
Management principles for acute attacks include removing precipitants, providing adequate carbohydrate, and giving haem therapy to suppress the overactive pathway, alongside symptom control
Porphyria cutanea tarda is managed by addressing iron overload and cofactors and by strict sun protection
reference.pathophysiology: Haem is synthesised through an eight-step enzymatic pathway; a partial deficiency of one of these enzymes, most relevant in the liver, causes a hepatic porphyria. In the acute porphyrias (such as acute intermittent porphyria from hydroxymethylbilane synthase deficiency), demand for haem induces the rate-controlling enzyme ALA synthase, and the downstream enzyme block leads to accumulation of the neurotoxic precursors delta-aminolaevulinic acid and porphobilinogen, producing neurovisceral attacks. Factors that increase hepatic haem demand, including many drugs metabolised by cytochrome P450, fasting, and steroid hormones, upregulate the pathway and precipitate attacks. In porphyria cutanea tarda, reduced hepatic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity, exacerbated by iron, alcohol, oestrogens, and hepatitis C, causes accumulation of photoactive porphyrins that damage sun-exposed skin. Chronic hepatic involvement predisposes to hepatocellular carcinoma.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary tyrosinaemia and other metabolic disorders
additionalInvestigations: Spot urine porphobilinogen and delta-aminolaevulinic acid during symptomatic acute episodes
Plasma, urine, and faecal porphyrin profiling to classify the porphyria type
Enzyme activity assays and genetic testing to confirm the specific defect
Testing for hepatitis C, iron studies, and HFE genotyping in porphyria cutanea tarda
Electrolytes to detect hyponatraemia during acute attacks
Hepatic imaging and alpha-fetoprotein surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma in acute porphyrias
redFlags: Acute attack with progressive motor weakness or bulbar and respiratory involvement threatening ventilatory failure
Severe hyponatraemia with seizures during an attack
Autonomic instability with marked hypertension and tachyarrhythmia
New hepatic mass suggesting hepatocellular carcinoma
reference.prognosis: With prompt recognition, removal of triggers, and appropriate treatment, acute attacks usually resolve, though severe attacks can cause lasting neurological deficits or death; recurrent attacks and chronic disease carry an increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma, while porphyria cutanea tarda generally responds well to treatment of underlying cofactors.
pitfalls: Failing to consider porphyria in recurrent unexplained severe abdominal pain, delaying diagnosis
Administering porphyrinogenic drugs that precipitate or worsen an acute attack
Restricting carbohydrate and calories during illness, which aggravates attacks
Omitting hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance in older patients with acute porphyria
